chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'We have a neighbor who is a teacher (of writing), and he asked me to ask you about his profession.' He said, 'Tell him that when the boy is handed over to him, he should say to his family: I am only teaching him writing and arithmetic, and I trade with him by teaching him the Quran, until his earnings are pleasing (pure and lawful).'

key_terms.يُكَتِّبُ: He teaches writing / He is a scribe

ai.seo_question: How does a teacher of writing ensure his earnings are considered halal and pure in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In the context of the *Kuttab* (scribal schools) era, this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the juristic concern of mixing secular livelihood with religious duty. The Imam advises the teacher to explicitly frame his commercial activity as trading in the 'skill of Quranic teaching,' thereby sanctifying his income and ensuring it is *tayyib* (pure/pleasant), a key criterion for lawful earnings in Shia fiqh.
